rows.question: Both fall detection papers use an ESP32. How does each one send its sensor data?
rows.expected: Adebesin et al.: the ESP32 sends over LoRa to a gateway; bathroom study: ESP32-C3 nodes send 2.56 s windows over Wi-Fi to a Raspberry Pi 4B
rows.answer: In the adebesin2026 wearable fall detection paper, the ESP32 handles LoRa communication with a gateway, transmitting acceleration and velocity readings via an RYLR896 UART LoRa transceiver module (868/915 MHz) attached to a Freenove ESP32-WROVER CAM board. [1][2] Its protocol stack uses CoAP over UDP, IPv6 and 6LoWPAN on LoRa, and the gateway forwards data via HTTP/TCP/IPv4 over Ethernet. [3] In the bathroom fall mmWave paper (arXiv 2603.17069), the ESP32-C3 nodes perform sensing, timestamping and lightweight preprocessing, then transmit buffered 2.56 s windows over Wi-Fi to a Raspberry Pi 4B edge gateway. [4] The two ESP32-C3 sensing nodes in that paper also share ESP32-based time synchronization. [5]

rows.question: What sampling rate does each fall detection paper use for its sensor data?
rows.expected: Adebesin et al.: 20 Hz (50 ms); bathroom study: streams mapped to a common 100 Hz
rows.answer: In adebesin2026 (wearable fall detection with LoRa), the wearable device's sensors are sampled at 20 Hz, with fall-detection experiments using a fixed 50 ms sampling period (equivalent to 20 Hz) and baseline activities using a dynamic period ranging from 500 ms to 50 ms. [1][2] Lower-frequency baseline streams in adebesin2026 were linearly resampled to a uniform 20 Hz before windowing. [3] In the arXiv 2603.17069 bathroom fall detection work, the mmWave radar node produced 3D point clouds at 12.5 Hz, while the vibration node sampled at 200 Hz and was resampled to 100 Hz. [4][5] In arXiv 2603.17069, the radar and vibration streams are mapped to a common rate of 100 Hz during preprocessing. [6]

rows.question: On the Raspberry Pi 4B, how does the end-to-end latency of the radar-only model compare with the radar and vibration fusion model in the bathroom study?
rows.expected: Radar only 28.4 ms vs fusion 15.8 ms
rows.answer: In the bathroom fall detection paper (arXiv 2603.17069), the Motion-Mamba radar-only model on the Raspberry Pi 4B has an end-to-end latency of 28.4 ms per 2.56 s window (7.5 ms preprocessing, 19.8 ms inference). [1] The radar and vibration fusion model has an end-to-end latency of 15.8 ms (8.9 ms preprocessing, 6.7 ms inference). [2] The fusion model is therefore 28.4 ms − 15.8 ms = 12.6 ms faster end-to-end, about 1.8× lower latency (28.4 / 15.8 ≈ 1.80). Its preprocessing is slightly slower (8.9 ms vs 7.5 ms), but its inference is much faster (6.7 ms vs 19.8 ms). [1][2] The paper also reports that the fusion model reduces latency from 35.9 ms for the strongest baseline to 15.8 ms on the Raspberry Pi 4B gateway. [3]
